ImageDescription.value: The Best Farm/L’Hermitage Slave Village site, Monocacy National Battlefield, Frederick, Maryland, USA, in early morning shadows. The house is an unusual example of a mixture of the local Federal style and Caribbean French Colonial styles of building and plantation culture, transplanted from Haiti/Saint-Domingue to central Maryland. It was built as the home of the Vincendrière family, who fled Saint-Domingue during the Haitian Revolution, and came to Maryland to establish a version of the plantation culture with which they were familiar. L'Hermitage was one of the largest slave-holding plantations in Maryland, and was notable for its brutal treatment of those enslaved there. The adjacent lands are documented as L'Hermitage Slave Village Archeological Site. The lands were fought over during the Battle of Monocacy in 1864 during the American Civil War. The hip-roofed barn, unusual for Maryland, is seen to the rear.Enoch Louis Lowe, 29th Governor of Maryland, was born at L'Hermitage in 1820, son of Bradley Samuel Adams Lowe and Adelaide Bellumeau de la Vincendrière

ImageDescription.value: Devonshire Lodge (Low-Martin House), Windsor, Ontario, Canada, 2025-08-31. Commissioned by the rum-runner Harry Low in 1927, the building was designed in the style of a Cotswold cottage and completed in 1928. It served as the home of Member of Parliament Paul Martin Sr. for almost three decades. It was designated under the Ontario Heritage Act in 2008.

ImageDescription.value:
Twin mills (front: green mill, 1856; rear: red mill or Schoof’s mill, 1706), Greetsiel, Krummhörn, Lower Saxony, Germany
The fishing village of Greetsiel is located in Krummhörn on the North Sea coast of East Frisia. It was founded in the Middle Ages as a small port and was shaped by crab fishing and trade for centuries. The historic town center with its 17th-century gabled houses and the harbour with its fleet of crab boats still give Greetsiel its maritime character today.
The Greetsiel twin mills at the entrance to the village are particularly well known. The two Dutch windmills date from the 19th century (1856 and 1921). They originally served as grain mills and were important components of regional agriculture. One of the mills burned down partially in 2019, but has been restored and rebuilt.
Today, the windmills are landmarks of the village. They can be visited and provide insights into traditional milling technology. Together with the historic harbour, they characterize the typical image of Greetsiel and symbolize East Frisian coastal culture.

Artist.value: Dietmar Rabich
